items.text:
Many things about Russia are hard to predict.

The result of this election wasn't one of them.

In a political system tightly controlled by the Kremlin, the party of power – United Russia –had been widely expected to remain the largest in parliament by a large margin.

There were no upsets. No surprises. No other party came close.

Preliminary results suggest that United Russia, which is supported by President Putin, is on course to retain its constitutional majority in the State Duma - with even bigger numbers than last time round.

And that's after more than four-and-half years of war on Ukraine, which have resulted in massive battlefield losses for the Russian army, economic difficulties and, most recently, widespread petrol shortages due to Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil facilities.

Those parties trailing far behind, but which have cleared the 5% threshold and made it into the new Duma, featured in the previous parliament, too: a Duma that was fully behind the Kremlin and the so-called special military operation.

One party that didn't make it into parliament was Yabloko.

Yabloko had been the only anti-war political party permitted to take part in the election - permission that was short-lived.

Just twelve days after being registered for the vote it was removed from the ballot (the party list) by the Supreme Court, an indication of Kremlin concern that Yabloko's pro-peace message was gaining too much traction with the public.

The party isn't surprised that the new Duma looks like being as pro-Kremlin as the previous one.

"What other result can there be if there were ten parties on the ballot and they all support the policies of Putin?" Yabloko party chairman Nikolai Rybakov tells me.

"I don't think the Duma will change. They'll vote 100% for the policies of Putin just like they did."

Although Yabloko had been struck off the party list, around a hundred of its candidates remained in individual constituency races. According to preliminary results, none have won seats. The party claims it has come under sustained pressure.

"Some of our candidates, who should have been running, are in jail, many were barred from running and some of our election observers weren't registered and were unable to keep an eye on the voting," Nikolai says.

Ahead of the final day of this three-day election, Ukraine launched a large-scale drone attack on the Moscow area. Three people were killed in Moscow Region, while in the capital the city's oil refinery was hit.

At a polling station near the oil refinery, I spoke to voters about the attack.

There was no sense of surprise. More a quiet resignation. With Russia's war on Ukraine now in its fifth year, Muscovites have grown used to their city periodically becoming a front line.

"People in the Donbas, as well as in Bryansk, and Belgorod near the Ukrainian border, hear this kind of thing every day," a voter called Viktor told me.

"And they just get on with their lives."

The outcome of this election was predictable. What happens next is less clear.

The Kremlin is likely to use the result to claim that most Russians have rallied behind the president, and to justify future policies and subsequent decisions on the course of the war.

The key question: what will those decisions be?

President Putin recently ruled out another wave of mobilisation.

"There is no scenario today that would require it," he declared.

Not today, then. But what about tomorrow?

Despite official denials, in Russian society there remains deep anxiety about the possibility of a new round of mobilisation.

At the very least, the Kremlin is likely to treat the election result as a 'mandate from the people' to continue the war.

items.title: 'Far from their best' to 'a joy to watch' -  ranking Premier League teams' start to season

We are five matches into the league season and there is a long
items.text:
There is now a three-week international break with no Premier League games until 10 October.

We are five matches into the league season and there is a long way to go in the campaign, but which teams have impressed so far and who have disappointed?

You can have your say in the comments at the bottom of the page.

Arsenal: Solid start to their title defence until they were ripped apart by Brighton having survived a penalty scare at Sunderland. 7

Aston Villa: Signs they are beginning to move in the right direction after losing so many key players during the transfer window. 6

Bournemouth: If games lasted 80 minutes the Cherries would be near the top of the table. Need to cut out conceding so late. 6

Brentford: Demolished Spurs and Chelsea without fuss during a highly impressive unbeaten start. Can they keep it up and challenge for Europe? 8

Brighton: Kings of entertainment after hitting 16 goals in five top-flight games, including three against champions Arsenal. A joy to watch. 9

Chelsea: After a strong start under Xabi Alonso, the Blues have lost two of their past three - and were picked apart by Brentford. Are they really moving in the right direction? 6

Coventry City: You could hear the sighs of relief in the away end at Nottingham Forest on Saturday. Will Frank Lampard's side kick on after that win? 6

Crystal Palace: Room for improvement after one win and three defeats. 5

Everton: Despite a transfer window to forget, David Moyes has made the Toffees hard to beat. 6

Fulham: Decent draws against Liverpool and Manchester United but need a win. Ipswich (away) followed by Hull (home), Coventry (away) and Crystal Palace (home) offer hope when they return from the international break. 5

Hull City: To have eight points from a tough opening five fixtures is an excellent return, including beating Manchester United and drawing with Aston Villa and Chelsea. 8

Ipswich Town: Defensively vulnerable but two late winners, against Sunderland and Crystal Palace, have earned them six points and shown their fighting spirit. 5

Leeds United: Fifth in the league, unbeaten and with the joint-best defensive record. They showed what they are capable of with a superb 4-1 win over Newcastle. 7

Liverpool: Unbeaten but have been far from their best. Three clean sheets in their past three games, but more is expected from Andoni Iraola's side. 6

Manchester City: Five league games, five victories. Managed to win at Manchester United despite going down to 10 men midway through the first half. With Erling Haaland already top scorer, City fans will expect a real push to win the league. 9

Manchester United: Disappointing performances to lose at Hull and draw at a Fulham side who were bottom of the league. Their only win so far came against Ipswich and they were denied a victory at Everton by a late equaliser. 4

Newcastle United: A mixed bag under new manager Matthias Jaissle. They impressed in a draw against Liverpool, won comfortably at Tottenham, but were also terrible in a loss at Leeds, although they responded well to beat Hull. 6

Nottingham Forest: Their best results have come away, drawing at Liverpool and winning at Aston Villa. But their home form will be a huge worry - yet to score a goal and with only one point from three matches at the City Ground. 5

Sunderland: After coming seventh in 2025-26, Sunderland fans will have wanted a better start to this season. The Black Cats gave good accounts of themselves against Arsenal and Manchester City, but lost both matches. 5

Tottenham Hotspur: After spending more than £300m in the summer, Spurs have been poor, failing to score in their opening four league matches. Supporters will be demanding an instant improvement after the international break. 2

items.title: Attention is all you have
items.author: zer0tonin
items.summary:
The Tetris effect is one of psychology’s most easy to reproduce experiments.
Simply spend a bit of time playing the eponymous game every day for a few
items.text:
The Tetris effect is one of psychology’s most easy to reproduce experiments.
Simply spend a bit of time playing the eponymous game every day for a few weeks.
After a little while, you’ll start recognizing familiar Tetromino shapes in clouds, buildings, and everyday objects.
You might even see them appear before your eyes when you start falling asleep.

Attention hijacking

There’s one lesson the Tetris effect teaches us: whatever you focus on long enough will end up shaping your thoughts.
This can be a good thing since it’s how we learn new skills and discover new ideas.
Sadly, less and less of our attention is focused intentionally.
Instead of picking what we want to see we let other people decide what is supposed to be good for us.

Do you want to watch a video?
YouTube knows you like cooking and art streams.
But why not also recommend a few clips about the stock market bubble, global warming, and the war in Iran.
Doomscrolling will make you stay longer and click on a few more ads.

Do you want to listen to music?
Just open a Spotify playlist and let the algorithm figure out what you like.
Please ignore the AI slop they will insert in between real songs to avoid paying royalties to real artists.

Do you want to know how your colleagues are doing?
Too bad, LinkedIn will bury any relevant career news between the opinion of complete strangers.
It is surely just a coincidence that those strangers happen to be shilling whatever Microsoft is invested in at the moment.

Do you want the opinion of strangers on a product?
Well those Redditors you wanted to ask are probably just a bunch of LLMs talking to a bunch of Russian trolls now.
I hope you didn’t value their opinion too much.

If, like me and most people, you spend the major part of your day focused on your device, there’s no doubt it’s affecting you.
And when you let someone else dictate what appears on your screen, it’s the same as giving them the key to your brain.

Back to an intentional internet

The internet wasn’t always like that.
Before recommendation algorithms were a thing, you had to decide what you would be doing on the computer.

You didn’t really have one big app that you could open and order it to entertain you.
Instead, you had a few dozen of bookmarks to websites, each with a specific idea in mind.
A site for video game news, that one website with lots of tutorials, a blog about anime that didn’t update often enough, a wiki about a TV show from the 90s…

Of course awful things existed on the web.
We had Encyclopedia Dramatica and Rotten.com, but you actually had to put the effort to go there if you wanted.
Nobody was going to put pictures of dead kids and far-right propaganda as a suggestion after a pancake recipe or a cat video.

The good thing is that this intentional internet is still around.
It has just been a bit buried below the corporate web, but it’s not very hard to find.
After all you’re on this blog, so you probably already have a good idea about it.

The main difference between this time and now is you.
When you want to get back to reading blogs, RSS feeds, and finish that tutorial instead of doomscrolling shorts, you have to get used to a slower internet.
One where content is not infinite and doesn’t get updated every click.

But like every habit, the only thing you have to do is to keep at it.
And if you pay enough attention to it, something will click in your brain.
